chunks: "The first reason is current per amp of load. In a buck the inductor carries the output current.
In a boost, energy conservation says the inductor carries the input current, I out over (1-D) , so for the same load current the inductor and switch carry more, and at a high boost ratio a lot more.
Conduction loss goes with current squared, so the DCR and R DS(on) losses get bigger.

To be precise, the inductor always sits on the low-voltage side, so at the same power and the same two voltages a buck and a boost have the same inductor current; the penalty shows up when you need the same load current, or a big ratio.
The second reason, and usually the biggest, is the diode. In a non-synchronous boost the diode carries the entire load current, so you lose V F times I out continuously.
A Schottky at 0. 4 volts and 1 amps is 0. 4 watts on a 5 watts output, 8% gone. In a buck the diode only conducts for (1-D) of the time, so the loss is smaller at high duty cycle.

Then there are secondary things: the output current is pulsed, so the capacitor has higher ripple current and loss, the switch node is at the output voltage, which is higher, and at high duty cycle the off-time gets short and losses climb fast.
To be fair, it isn't fundamental. With a synchronous boost and similar parts, the loss budget is close to a synchronous buck at the same power.
The penalty shows up mostly with non-synchronous parts and high ratios."
